lines.text: A land of copper and frankincense, mud-brick forts and sailors who built an empire across the sea. This is the story of Oman.
About five thousand years ago, Bronze Age people raised stone towers and beehive-shaped tombs at Bat, Al-Khutm and Al-Ayn.
The Sumerians knew this land as Magan, a place of copper miners, and traded with it across the Gulf.
In the thirteenth century the great mud-brick fort of Bahla rose in the interior, one of many forts guarding the land.
In the seventeen hundreds a new dynasty took power, and the sultanate of Oman we know today began to take shape.
That family was the Al Said, and it has ruled Oman ever since, from 1744 to today.
Said bin Sultan ruled both Oman and the island of Zanzibar off East Africa, and moved his court there.
After his death in 1856, Zanzibar became a sultanate of its own, ruled by his heirs, a great centre of the spice and slave trade.
In 1970 Qaboos bin Said became sultan, and in fifty years he turned Oman into a modern state.
His cousin, Haitham bin Tariq, would succeed him as sultan in 2020.
In Muscat, work began on a great mosque bearing Qaboos's name, which opened in 2001.
And in 2000 the frankincense trees and old ports of Dhofar, the heart of the ancient incense trade, became a World Heritage Site.
From copper and incense to a modern sultanate, Oman has always looked to the sea and the world beyond.
